extracted.intended_audience: scholars and students of Aristotelian poetics, philosophy of literature, and drama/theatre theory
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting and applying Aristotle's criteria for tragedy and comedy (character types, kinds of error, emotions aroused, structural parts like recognition/reversal, and the possibility of catharsis). Useful for literary-theory analysis of dramatic plots and comic/tragic emotions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Objects imitated: serious vs frivolous characters
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragedy and comedy clearly imitate different objects: human character is either serious (σπουδαίους) or frivolous (φαύλους); characters in drama must be 'better (βελτίονας) or worse (χείρονας) than us or such (τοιούτους) as us' (Poetics 2. 1448a1-5,16-18).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this distinction to classify dramatic characters: tragic protagonists represent the serious/better-than-usense, comic protagonists the frivolous/worse-than-usense. But the paper stresses these categories still allow for strong likeness to the audience (see 'intermediate' character criterion).

rubrics_metrics.name: Tragic protagonist: intermediate character and error
rubrics_metrics.description: A tragedy ought not to represent excellent characters falling into bad fortune nor extremely knavish characters; rather it should represent an intermediate character (ὁ μεταξὺ) who is neither distinguished in virtue nor depraved, but 'makes a mistake' (δι᾽ ἁμαρτίαν τινά) (Poetics 13. 1453a7-10).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Protagonist should be plausible and human (not saintly or monstrous). The source of the tragic action is an error, not vice; this error renders the figure like us and grounds pity/fear.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comic protagonist: frivolous but not vicious; error-based ridiculousness
rubrics_metrics.description: Comic characters are of the more frivolous sort (φαυλοτέρων) but 'not frivolous in accordance with any vice (οὐ . . . κατὰ πᾶσαν κακίαν)'; 'the ridiculous (τὸ . . . γελοῖον . . .) is a mistake (ἁμάρτημά . . .) and a thing shameful (αἶσχος) but painless and not destructive' (Poetics 5. 1449a32-35).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comic protagonists should err in ways that are shameful/ridiculous yet harmless — the error, not moral depravity, produces the comic action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nature of error: destructive/painful vs painless/not destructive
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragic error issues in action that is 'destructive or painful' (πρᾶξις φθαρτικὴ ἢ ὀδυνηρά) — death, severe pains, wounds; comic error is 'painless and not destructive' (Poetics passages cited).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating or composing a plot, determine whether the central error threatens/causes physical harm (tragic register) or merely ill repute/shame without physical harm (comic register).

rubrics_metrics.name: Emotions aroused by tragedy: pity (ἔλεος) and fear (φόβος)
rubrics_metrics.description: Aristotle: pity concerns the undeserved (περὶ τὸν ἀνάξιον) falling into bad fortune, and fear concerns the likeness (περὶ τὸν ὅμοιον). Rhetoric: pity is 'a pain felt at the appearance of a bad thing, destructive or painful, happening to someone who does not deserve it' (1385b13-14); fear is 'a pain or distress arising from an image of something bad, destructive or painful, that is going to happen' (1382a20-21).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess scenes by whether they instantiate undeserved suffering (pity) or provoke audience identification and anticipatory dread (fear). Proximity/likeness affects which emotion dominates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emotions aroused by comedy: ridicule and shame (analogy to pity/fear)
rubrics_metrics.description: Schollmeier's thesis: as pity and fear attend tragic action, so ridicule and shame attend comic action. Ridicule is a pain/distress felt at appearance of ill repute befalling another; shame is a pain/distress about the appearance of ill repute for oneself or close others (Rhetoric 2.6.1383b12-14). Ridicule is linked to undeserved ill repute; shame to likeness/proximity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this mapping to analyse comic scenes: judge whether the comic action produces ridicule (for non-intimates) or shame (when the mistaken figure is close to or resembles us).

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of undeservedness and likeness in emotional responses
rubrics_metrics.description: Pity concerns undeserved suffering; fear concerns likeness to us. Analogously, ridicule concerns undeserved ill repute; shame concerns likeness or closeness to us. If the sufferer is very close, fear/shame may replace pity/ridicule (Rhetoric examples).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating audience effect, consider both whether the harm/reproach is deserved and how closely the character resembles or is related to the audience's self or intimates; these dimensions determine the emotional response.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognition (ἀναγνώρισις) as structural element
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognition is 'a change from ignorance to knowledge (ἐξ ἀγνοίας εἰς γνῶσιν), and either to friendship or to enmity, in those destined for good fortune or bad fortune' (Poetics 11. 1452a29-32).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognition can transform the moral/relational status of characters and is a key device to alter the emotional valence of actions (e.g., discovering kinship prevents intended harm). Use recognition to enable purgation of tragic/comic qualities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reversal (περιπέτεια) as structural element
rubrics_metrics.description: Reversal is 'a change to the opposite (εἰς τὸ ἐναντίον) in the things being done' (Poetics 11. 1452a22-23); a change of fortune in the action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reversal, often combined with recognition, produces the dénouement that can purge an action's pitiable/fearful or ridiculous/shameful qualities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Catharsis via recognition + reversal
rubrics_metrics.description: Aristotle implies (Poetics) that the most beautiful tragedies are those where recognition brings reversal; such configurations can purge the action's pitiableness and fearfulness. By analogy, a comedy can purge its ridiculousness and shamefulness through recognition and reversal — i.e., comic catharsis is possible if the action includes these parts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether a plot's structural devices (recognition/reversal) resolve the central error so the audience experiences a 'purgation' or resolution of the relevant emotions. Note Scholarly caveats: extant ancient comedies often lack such devices; Shakespearean examples provide modern analogues (e.g., Comedy of Errors).

rubrics_metrics.name: Single vs double action: double action favors comic pleasure
rubrics_metrics.description: Aristotle argues that a composition with a double action yields a pleasure 'more appropriate for comedy' (ἡδονὴ . . . μᾶλλον τῆς κωμῳδίας οἰεία) (Poetics 13. 1453a35-36). Example: the Odyssey brings opposite endings for better and worse characters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When composing/evaluating comedy, consider multiple interlocked actions (double action) that allow contrasting fortunes (rise/fall) — these structures are conducive to comic pleasure per Aristotle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comic action as rise from bad fortune to good
rubrics_metrics.description: Schollmeier's conjecture: comedy portrays a character rising from bad fortune to good because of a mistake (author's explicit proposal), paralleling tragic action but with opposite direction of fortune change.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge comic plots by whether central action moves toward better fortune for protagonists (even if the improvement is avoided at dénouement through recognition), driven by a harmless mistake rather than vice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tragic action includes suffering actions among intimates
rubrics_metrics.description: Aristotle: seek actions where sufferings occur among friends/relatives (e.g., brother kills brother, son father, etc.) — these are actions 'to be sought' as sources of tragedy (Poetics 14. 1453b19-22).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In tragic composition, emphasize actions that threaten or enact intimate harm — these generate strong pity and fear when combined with undeservedness and likeness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ridiculous as a species of the shameful; comic mask example
rubrics_metrics.description: Aristotle: 'Of the shameful (τοῦ αἰσχροῦ) the ridiculous (τὸ γελοῖον) is a part (μόριον)' and 'a ridiculous mask (τὸ γελοῖον πρόσωπον) is at once shameful (αἰσχρόν) and contorted without being painful' (Poetics 5. 1449a33-37).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use physical exaggeration and distorted appearance (mask, gesture) to manifest the ridiculous/shameful quality without invoking real pain — design comic display to signal shamefulness that is non-destructive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proximity/relationship effects on pity/fear and ridicule/shame
rubrics_metrics.description: Aristotle (Rhetoric) notes we pity those we know if not too closely related; if too close, we 'feel for them as we feel for ourselves' (fear for self example). Similarly, shame is felt before those for whom we would be ashamed (those whom we teach, advise, or compete with).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider audience identification and social relations: closeness can shift the felt emotion from pity-->fear or ridicule-->shame. Use character relationships to modulate audience affect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dramatic imitation and pleasurable learning
rubrics_metrics.description: Drama is imitation only; actors 'do as if' and do not actually harm. Aristotle: we take pleasure in making and observing imitations; learning from imitation is pleasant (Poetics 3-4. 1448a/b).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Account for the paradox of pleasurable painful emotions (tragic pity/fear, comic ridicule/shame) by emphasizing the mediated, mimetic nature of drama; the audience's safe distance enables enjoyment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Best tragedies/comedies employ 'beautiful' handling of myth via recognition/reversal
rubrics_metrics.description: Aristotle: dramatists ought to employ traditional tragic myths 'beautifully' (καλῶς) by incorporating recognition and reversal; the most beautiful tragedy/comedy has actions structured to produce appropriate catharsis (Poetics 14. 1453b25-26).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess quality by whether a playwright integrates recognition and reversal in service of emotional purgation; mere sensational outcomes without structural realization are deficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comic catharsis is contested but possible in complex plots
rubrics_metrics.description: Schollmeier argues comic catharsis is possible when recognition and reversal purge ridiculousness/shamefulness; scholars disagree (Else denies comic catharsis; Cooper/Janko offer audience-centered accounts). Extant classical comedies often lack examples, but Shakespearean/comic-epic examples (Comedy of Errors) show recognition-driven resolution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When claiming comic catharsis, require evidence of plot devices (recognition/reversal) that resolve the humiliating error; distinguish catharsis-as-structural-purge from catharsis-as-audience-experience.
